correctness.rationale: For every nonnegative integer polynomial of degree d>=2 and a>=2, its leading degree-d monomial guarantees at least a total coefficient mass outside any single binomial coefficient in g(Y+a-1). This proves all translated coefficients are legal base-b digits for b=g(a)-a+1; their sum g(a) proves the second fixed point, and the first follows from g(a)=b+(a-1). The explicit 9j+7 and 9j+4 quadratic identities have legal digits for their stated j, hence yield two disjoint positive-density base families. Exact finite checks separately confirm 11,880 polynomial cases and 3,999 base-family cases, but the infinite proof is symbolic.

broader_coverage.reasoning: A general finite localization algorithm decides each fixed base, and fixed-base finiteness is known. Neither provides the varying-base carry-free identity for every nonnegative degree-two-or-higher polynomial, nor a density-two-ninths lower bound for square-map base obstructions.

The fixed-base finiteness theorem does not imply infinitely many exceptional bases; the decimal-only cycle analysis cannot quantify exceptional bases.

value.rationale: The motivating arithmetic-dynamics theory identifies injectivity of the cycle-to-residue projection as the precise condition for congruence basins and gives finite base tables. The theorem exhibits noninjectivity for infinitely many bases for every nonnegative polynomial generator of degree >=2, and for a fixed square generator forces it on at least two-ninths of bases. A uniform, positive-density structural statement is not a pointwise finite search, arbitrary slice, or simple reformulation of the existing local semiconjugacy.
